rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The people have recognized their sin after mixing righteous acts with evil, and God may still accept their repentance.
rows.anchor: have become conscious of their sinning after having done righteous deeds side by side with evil ones; [136] [and] it may well be that God will accept their repentance

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here sadaqah primarily means zakah, the obligatory purifying dues on Muslims whose property or income reaches a minimum.
rows.anchor: it primarily denotes the tax called zakah ("the purifying dues") incumbent on every Muslim enjoying a certain minimum of property and/or income

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A state's acceptance of zakah recognizes the giver as a Muslim in the Qur'anic sense.
rows.anchor: amounts to a recognition of the giver as a "Muslim" in the Qur'anic sense of this term

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet refused zakah from people whose conduct exposed them as hypocrites.
rows.anchor: the Prophet refused to accept it from all whose behaviour had made it obvious that they were hypocrites

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse authorizes the Prophet and later Islamic authorities to accept zakah from people who demonstrate repentance through deeds.
rows.anchor: to accept the payment of zakah from those who express their repentance by deeds as well as by

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hud's compatriots insinuate that a god has afflicted him with madness.
rows.anchor: I.e., with madness.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad also renders the oath as Hud's declaration that he is guiltless of their associating others with God, rejecting their sarcastic madness claim.
rows.anchor: thus rejecting the sardonic suggestion of his compatriots that one of their imaginary deities might have stricken him with madness

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hud's challenge closely resembles the challenge in the final sentence of 7:195.
rows.anchor: a very similar challenge in the last sentence of 7:195

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Being held by the forelock means that every living being is fully controlled by God and depends entirely on Him.
rows.anchor: there is no living being over which He has not complete control and which is not entirely dependent on Him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ancient Arabs used the forelock-in-another's-hand idiom for a person's humility and subjection.
rows.anchor: the ancient Arabs used to say, "The forelock of so-and-so is in the hand of so-and-so"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad connects the expression with 11:6, where he has discussed God's control over living beings.
rows.anchor: complete control and which is not entirely dependent on Him (cf. verse 6 of this surah)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The same idiom occurs in 96:15-16, its first occurrence in chronological revelation order.
rows.anchor: 96:15-16, where this idiomatic expression occurs for the first time in the chronological order of Qur'anic revelation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God governs by ultimate truth and justice, ensures evildoers face consequences and righteousness is rewarded in this world and the hereafter.
rows.anchor: He governs all that exists in accordance with a system of truth and justice in the ultimate, absolute sense of these terms

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur'an does not explicitly call Abraham's guests angels; because rusuluna often means heavenly messengers, classical commentators identify them as angels.
rows.anchor: term rusuluna ("Our messengers") is often used in the sense of heavenly messengers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The glad tidings mentioned in this passage are explained at 11:71.
rows.anchor: For the contents of the "glad tiding" referred to here, see verse 71 below

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham's later plea for Sodom explains why the story of Abraham precedes the story of Lot.
rows.anchor: The reason for prefacing the story of Lot with an episode from Abraham's life lies in the latter's subsequent pleading in behalf of the sinful people of Sodom

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad suggests Abraham's promised leadership may have heightened his responsibility for his family and for Lot's people.
rows.anchor: possibly, in God's earlier promise to him, "Behold, I shall make thee a leader of men"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad directs readers to his parallel discussion of Shu'ayb in surah 7, note 67.
rows.anchor: See surah 7, note 67.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage places belief in one God and justice in human dealings together as twin requirements of righteousness.
rows.anchor: belief in the One God and justice in all dealings between man and man (see surah 6, note 150) are here placed together as the twin postulates of all righteousness

rows.speaker: Some commentators
rows.claim: Some commentators describe Madyan's people as commercially minded and prone to fraudulent dealings.
rows.anchor: Some commentators assume that the people of Madyan were of a particularly commercial bent of mind, and given to fraudulent dealings

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad rejects a merely historical reading: the passage teaches that righteousness toward God requires moral and social righteousness toward people.
rows.anchor: the purport of this passage and of its sequence goes far beyond anything that might be construed by a purely "historical" interpretation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The next verse restates the prohibition positively as an injunction to give full measure and weight.
rows.anchor: the above prohibition is re-stated in a positive form, as an injunction, in the next verse

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad notes that the literal wording is plural: "Do thy prayers command thee?"
rows.anchor: Lit., "Do thy prayers command thee...", etc.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The people's desired freedom to use their wealth ignores others' rights and needs, especially those of the poor; this explains their sarcasm about Shu'ayb.
rows.anchor: without regard to the rights and needs of others, especially the poor: hence their sarcastic reference, in the next sentence, to Shu'ayb's clemency and right-mindedness

rows.speaker: Zamakhshari, Razi and several other commentators
rows.claim: Zamakhshari, Razi, and other commentators treat the bracketed clause as elliptically implied in Shu'ayb's reply.
rows.anchor: Zamakhshari, Razi and several other commentators, the clause interpolated here between brackets is elliptically implied in Shu'ayb's answer

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Shu'ayb mentions God's ample worldly gifts to show that self-interest does not motivate his demand for fair dealings.
rows.anchor: His stress on the fact that God has graced him amply with worldly goods is meant to remind his countrymen that it is not self-interest

words: وَمَآ أُرِيدُ أَنْ أُخَالِفَكُمْ إِلَىٰ مَآ أَنْهَىٰكُمْ عَنْهُ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Shu'ayb says he does not intend to deprive them of what rightfully belongs to them, referring to 11:85.
rows.anchor: I do not aim at depriving you of what is rightfully yours

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad allows "His is the call of truth" or true invocation to God alone; al-haqq names God as Ultimate Reality, so prayer is directed to Him and invoking anything else is futile.
rows.anchor: expression da'wat al-haqq may be understood in the sense of "prayer directed towards Him who is the Ultimate Reality"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad also renders the phrase as "side by side with God."
rows.anchor: Or: "side by side with God".

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad explains that the literal expression is "his two palms."
rows.anchor: Lit., "his two palms".

rows.speaker: Zamakhshari
rows.claim: Yasjud is a metonym for complete submission to God's will, understood here as submission to the natural laws He decreed.
rows.anchor: yasjud ("prostrates himself" or "prostrate themselves") is a metonym for complete submission to His will (Zamakhshari)

rows.speaker: most of the classical commentators
rows.claim: They identify willing submitters as angels and believers, while deniers unwillingly remain subject to God's will without knowing it.
rows.anchor: According to most of the classical commentators, those who submit to God willingly (i.e., consciously) are the angels and the believers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because shadows are mentioned next, Asad takes man to include all physical things, animate and inanimate, not only conscious beings.
rows.anchor: it is logical to assume that the relative pronoun man relates in this context not merely to conscious beings but also to all other physical objects

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A material object's shadow changes with the sun's position; its morning and evening lengthening visibly expresses subjection to God's creative will.
rows.anchor: varying lengths of the shadow projected by any material object depend on the position of the sun in relation to the earth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad adds "once-dry" because awdiyah lacks the definite article al.
rows.anchor: The interpolation of the adjective "once-dry" before "river-beds" (awdiyah) is necessitated by the absence of the definite article al before this noun

rows.speaker: Zamakhshari
rows.claim: The indefinite form indicates that this rain fills only some riverbeds, leaving others dry.
rows.anchor: According to Zamakhshari, this indicates that only some of the river-beds are streaming with water while others, not affected by this particular rainfall, remain dry

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wad normally means a usually dry watercourse or riverbed that carries water after heavy rain, and by extension can mean a river.
rows.anchor: term wad (or wadi in popular parlance) denotes, primarily, a "water-course" or "river-bed" which is normally dry

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad supplies the ellipsis that clear water remains beneath the scum.
rows.anchor: while the water beneath remains clear

rows.speaker: other commentators
rows.claim: Other commentators make the opening of 13:18 an independent sentence: those who respond to God have the ultimate good.
rows.anchor: According to other commentators, the beginning of verse 18 is independent of the last sentence of the preceding verse

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad prefers Zamakhshari's reading, with al-husna qualifying the believers' response, because it explains the repeated reference to God's parables.
rows.anchor: Zamakhshari's reading - in which the expression al-husna is regarded as an adjective qualifying the believers' response - is preferable

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad's literal rendering of the phrase is "and the like of it with it."
rows.anchor: Lit., "and the like of it with it".

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad links the ransom phrase with 3:91 and its corresponding note 71.
rows.anchor: Cf. 3:91 and the corresponding note 71.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad translates sayhah as a blast of God's punishment and refers readers to his discussion at surah 11, note 98.
rows.anchor: term sayhah, rendered by me as "blast of [God's punishment"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad identifies the road as running from northern Hijaz to Syria along the Dead Sea; aerial photographs published by the American School of Oriental Research confirmed its trace.
rows.anchor: The existence of that road, which led from northern Hijaz to Syria, skirting the Dead Sea

rows.speaker: Zamakhshari
rows.claim: One Zamakhshari reading stresses God's creative power: a once-inert sperm-drop becomes articulate and able to argue clearly and courageously.
rows.anchor: Zamakhshari, "one interpretation is that after having been a (mere] drop of sperm

rows.speaker: Zamakhshari
rows.claim: His other reading is that a human may contend against his Sustainer and refuse to acknowledge the Creator.
rows.anchor: According to Zamakhshari and Razi, the above phrase is liable to two interpretations

rows.speaker: Razi
rows.claim: Razi unequivocally supports the first reading because the passage emphasizes evidence for a wise Creator, not human insolence or ingratitude.
rows.anchor: Razi, on his part, gives his. unqualified. support to the first of these two interpretations

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad regards both readings as complementary: rationality can raise humans to great achievements or lead them astray, as 36:77-78 illustrates.
rows.anchor: I am of the opinion that the above two interpretations are not mutually exclusive but, rather, complementary
